title: A Paleoarchaean impact crater in the Pilbara Craton, Western Australia

paper_content.abstract: The role of meteorite impacts in the origin, modification, and destruction of crust during the first two billion years of Earth history (4.5–2.5 billion years ago; Ga) is disputed. Whereas some argue for a relatively minor contribution overall, others have proposed that individual giant impactors (>10–50 km diameter) can initiate subduction zones and deep mantle plumes, arguably triggering a chain of events that formed cratons, the ancient nuclei of the continents. The uncertainty is compounded by the seeming absence of impact structures older than 2.23 Ga, such that the evidence for the terrestrial impact flux in the Hadean and Archaean eons is circumstantial. Here, we report the discovery of shatter cones in a complex, dominantly metasedimentary layer, the Antarctic Creek Member (ACM), in the centre of the East Pilbara Terrane, Western Australia, which provide unequivocal evidence for a hypervelocity meteorite impact. The shocked rocks of the crater floor are overlain by (unshocked) carbonate breccias and pillow lavas, stratigraphically constraining the age of the impact to 3.47 Ga and confirming discovery of the only Archaean crater known thus far.
paper_content.introduction:
With more than a million craters exceeding 1 km in diameter, and around forty more than 100 km across1,2, the Moon preserves an exquisite record of the intense bombardment endured by bodies in the inner solar system during the first billion years or so of its history (Fig. 1a)3. On Earth, this early impact record has seemingly been lost, reflecting the destructive efficiency of erosion and subduction in recycling primary (basaltic, oceanic) crust back into the convecting mantle. Nevertheless, the oldest parts of many cratons, the ancient Archaean (4.0–2.5 billion years ago; Ga) nuclei of the continents, formed at or before 3.5 Ga4, and should preserve some evidence for an impact flux that would have exceeded that of a similar area of the Moon of comparable age5–7 (Fig. 1a). However, the oldest recognized terrestrial impact structure, at Yarrabubba, Western Australia, is dated at 2.23 Ga8. Where are all the Archaean craters?

Finding direct evidence for Archaean impacts (i.e., craters or impact structures8), and thereby better constraining the Archaean impact flux, is important. Large impactors (here bodies > or >> 10 km in diameter) travelling in excess of 10 km s–1 deliver enormous quantities of kinetic energy, most of which will decay to heat, warming the crust and upper mantle9, with potential consequences for plausible tectonic modes on the early Earth10,11. Further, numerical models have shown that individual bolide impacts can instigate subduction, mantle upwellings (plumes), and voluminous production of primary (basaltic) crust12–14. Moreover, impacts provide a ready mechanism to fracture (brecciate) the crust and, in the presence of a hydrosphere15, drive intense hydrothermal alteration of this regolith, concentrating key mineral deposits16. Notably, impact craters may have provided the physical and chemical environments required for life to emerge on Earth and elsewhere17,18.

The East Pilbara Terrane (EPT), part of the Pilbara Craton of Western Australia, is a near-pristine, approximately 200 km diameter fragment of (mostly) Paleoarchaean (3.53–3.23 Ga) cratonic crust comprising domes of sodic granite (TTG) separated by steeply-inclined greenstone belts dominated by ultrabasic to basic volcanic rocks19 (Fig. 1b). Many interpret the EPT as a long-lived volcanic plateau formed by polyphase plume-driven magmatism, probably involving short-lived episodes of (proto)subduction19–21. More recently, it has been argued that the EPT ultimately formed at the site of a large bolide impact22, and that such an origin for the initiation of cratons may be generally applicable22,23.

Here, we report the discovery of an impact crater at the North Pole Dome, near the centre of the EPT (Fig. 1b, c). Exceptionally preserved shatter cones within a dominantly siliciclastic horizon (Fig. 2a, b), the Antarctic Creek Member (ACM), which has previously been shown to contain spherules (quenched and devitrified impact-melt droplets)24,25, provide unequivocal evidence for a hypervelocity meteorite impact 3.47 billion years ago. Both spherules and shatter cones are found within the same siliciclastic unit within the ACM, requiring at least two (one proximal, one distal) Paleoarchaean or earlier impact events7,26.
paper_content.results:
The North Pole Dome and Antarctic Creek Member (ACM)

At the base of the Pilbara Supergroup, the 10–15 km thick Warrawoona Group is dominated by weakly metamorphosed ultramafic to mafic volcanic rocks with subordinate felsic volcanic/volcaniclastic rocks and chert19 (Fig. 1b, c). Pillow lavas near its base are pervasively hydrothermally altered and cut by chert–barite veins and overlain by chemical sediments (mostly chert) containing the oldest known (stromatolite) fossils27. At higher stratigraphic levels, within the core of a structural dome (the North Pole Dome; Fig. 1c), a 2–3 km thick sequence of ultramafic–mafic volcanic rocks (the Mount Ada Basalt) contains a thin (up to 20 m) sedimentary unit, the Antarctic Creek Member, which consists of (silicified and carbonate-altered) felsic to mafic volcaniclastic rocks, chert, argillite, arenite and jaspilite intruded by dolerite19,28.

The ACM preserves evidence for the oldest known meteorite impact in the form of one or more layers containing spherules19,24, interpreted by most as globally-distributed airfall impact ejecta19,24,25,29,30, but whose petrogenesis is debated31,32. It contains detrital zircon grains with 207Pb/206Pb ages of 3470±2 Ma24, providing a maximum depositional age, but has not been dated directly. However, underlying felsic rocks near the base of the Mount Ada Basalt (3469±3 Ma), and at the base of the overlying sequence of felsic volcanic rocks (the Duffer Formation; 3468±2 Ma) constrain deposition of the ACM to around 3470 Ma (3469.2+1.8/–1.2 Ma; ref. 19).

Fieldwork in 2021 in a small area of the North Pole Dome identified shatter cones throughout most of the thickness of the ACM (Fig. 2a; Supplementary Fig. 1). The shatter cones crop out more-or-less continuously for at least several hundred metres extending broadly northeast from where the ACM crosses the track at 21° 02’ 54” S, 119° 23’ 35” E (Fig. 1c). At outcrop, the variably curved surfaces of the shatter cones are smooth, with divergent and branching ribs and a mean apical angle of around 90° (Fig. 2a; Supplementary Information Fig. 1a–d; see also a 3D model at: https://sketchfab.com/3d-models/shatter-cone-2-cd89206c6d6b4765be766659a6e377da), similar to the average of literature values33. Although the orientation of individual cone axes varies, almost all are steeply inclined and splay (the ribs diverge) downwards (Fig. 2a; Supplementary Fig. 1a–d)33, consistent with a right-way-up stratigraphy19. On a larger scale, the cones are clearly visible as hut-like structures, some several metres tall, which extend across the hillside (Supplementary Fig. 1e).

Immediately overlying the shocked (shatter cone-bearing) ACM is a 5–10 m thick stratabound sequence of polymictic carbonate breccias (occupying the more strongly eroded gully in Supplementary Information Fig. 1e) containing angular fragments of underlying rocks, conspicuously chert (Supplementary Information Fig. 2). The stratabound layer of carbonate breccias is clearly distinct from the (very recent) calcrete deposits that cover the surface of many exposures, and includes distinctive orange dykes up to a metre thick (Supplementary Fig. 2b) that extend for many tens of metres into the footwall. Directly overlying the carbonate breccias are hydrothermally altered basalts (the upper part of the Mount Ada Basalt), which are pillowed near their base (Supplementary Fig. 1e, f) and contain layers of chert at higher stratigraphic levels. We have found no shatter cones in either the pillow basalts or carbonate breccias/dykes.
paper_content.methods: We combine field observations and deductive reasoning with published geochronological data from the Geological Survey of Western Australia GSWA, as summarized in ref. 19.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
A review of “A Paleoarchean impact in the Pilbara Craton, Western Australia” by G. R. Osinski.
It was a pleasure to read this revised version of a previous manuscript submitted to [REDACTED]. The authors have done a
good job of addressing the comments of all three reviewers, which strengthens their case for shatter cones in ~3.47 Ga
rocks, which I agree provides the first evidence of a preserved meteorite impact crater in the Archaean. I will restate that this
is an important and exciting discovery.
Below I provide a series minor comments on the manuscript, which I hope the authors will find useful.
My one major comment is about the location of the shatter cones and their abundance. This was also raised by me and other
reviewers in the original manuscript and needs to be addressed. Science requires that observations are reproducible, which
for field geology, means that somebody else needs to be able to view these same rocks. The authors need to provide UTM
coordinates (on lines 101-102) and label (e.g., with a star) the location of the shatter cones on Figure 1. In addition, they
need to state how many outcrops they have documented shatter cones in.
While the authors may wish to keep these outcrops secret, this location data needs to be published to support their
arguments. I would also like to add, to the authors and editor, that I was approached by another high-ranking journal last
week to review a manuscript on what appear to be these very same shatter cones based on the abstract that was provided. I
wanted to complete this review first before accepting this potentially competing review.
L37: It would be good to add to this sentence that these spherule layers represent distal ejecta as some readers may not be
familiar with what these deposits are.
L41-44: I might suggest some slight rewording here – although I am uncertain if the numbers exist – but a large amount
(perhaps most) of the kinetic energy transferred to the crust ends up melting large volumes of rock (producing impact melt).
L57-59: It would be easier to follow and more consistent if the legend labelled the dashed black line as the Antarctic Creek
Member rather than “spherule-bearing chert”.
L71: Similar to the previous comment, to avoid confusion, mention the ACM here first, rather than on line 74. You should also
define this acronym again upon first mention in the main body of the text.
L94: I think you need a ) after “2 Ma”.
L97-99> I’m not sure of the journal’s requirements, but it’s usually best to state what the scale is for each sub-image, even if
obvious. So a finger for a, an x-com long rock hammer for b. What about c?
L101: The placement of the refs 39-41 reads like these papers discovered the shatter cones in question. I would split this
sentence. First state you identified the shatter cones, and then make it more explicit for the uninformed reader: state that
shatter cones are the only macroscopic shock metamorphic indicator, and then use those 39-41 refs. See also my comment
above about providing UTM coordinates and identifying the location of the shatter cones on Figure 1.
L103: I read their response to my previous comment about the potentially glassy shatter cone surface, but I would remove
this here. Not only do they not provide evidence, why/how could this surface still be glassy after 3.5 billion years. The
spherules certainly are not.
L143: This is difficult to assess as the authors have not provided information on the location of these shatter cones and their
abundance (i.e., number of outcrops).
L149: These breccias look far to coarse-grained to be airfall deposits. You could just shorten this and remove some
speculation by shortening to just say “impact-related products”.
L157-159: Given the authors have documented evidence for two large impacts within 10 Ma of each other at a single
location, (b) and (c) seem much more likely. I’ll let the authors decide if they want to make a bolder statement to this effect.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Dear Authors,
I think your finding of Archean shatter cones is very interesting and an important discovery. However, I find the manuscript
lacking some important information, i.e., more detailed investigations are needed in order to support many of the claims in
the manuscript.
The major issues that I see are:
1) the lack of a detailed description of the shatter cone distribution and relation to geological units. The authors claim that the
crater has a diameter of at least 100 km, based on the width of the North Pole Dome, but are shatter cones found on the
whole of the dome? It is from the current text highly unclear what the spatial distribution is (the area is not even marked on
the map)?
2) The authors claim that the shatter cone area to be situated on the flank of a central uplift? This needs to be supported by
better field evidence.
3) The authors speculate that the carbonate breccia represents crater fill, but this is not supported by any hard evidence, one
would expect highly shocked material and injected veins of melt rock in this, but this is not presented.
4) I do not understand the purpose of including the overlying spherule bed in the manuscript, how is this relevant to this
study?
5) Geologic and petrographic descriptions throughout the manuscript are sparse and insufficient.
Unless the authors cannot present better evidence supporting their claims of a very large and old impact structure, then I
think this should not be published in Nature Communications.
Best regards,
Carl Alwmark

Response to reviewer comments (NGS-2024-10-02678-T)
We are grateful to the expert reviewers for their comments, and provide our responses
(in red) below.
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
A review of “A Paleoarchean impact in the Pilbara Craton, Western Australia” by G. R.
Osinski.
It was a pleasure to read this revised version of a previous manuscript submitted to
[REDACTED]. The authors have done a good job of addressing the comments of all thre
e reviewers, which strengthens their case for shatter cones in ~3.47 Ga rocks,
which I agree provides the first evidence of a preserved meteorite impact crater in the
Archaean. I will restate that this is an important and exciting discovery.
We are pleased that the reviewer sees the importance of our observations and
considers that we have done a good job in responding to the former comments.
Below I provide a series minor comments on the manuscript, which I hope the authors
will find useful.
My one major comment is about the location of the shatter cones and their abundance.
This was also raised by me and other reviewers in the original manuscript and needs to
be addressed. Science requires that observations are reproducible, which for field
geology, means that somebody else needs to be able to view these same rocks. The
authors need to provide UTM coordinates (on lines 101-102) and label (e.g., with a star)
the location of the shatter cones on Figure 1. In addition, they need to state how many
outcrops they have documented shatter cones in.
We have mapped the shatter cones over a distance of a few hundred metres from
where they cross the track at 21 02’ 54” S, 119 23’ 35” E to the northeast. The shatter
cones crop out almost continuously over that distance, and continue into the hills. We
have added a sentence (beginning line 102 of the revised version) to clarify this:
“The shatter cones crop out more-or-less continuously for at least several hundred
metres extending broadly northeast from where the ACM crosses the track at 21 02’
54” S, 119 23’ 35” E”.
We have now added the location of the studied outcrops on Fig. 1c.
While the authors may wish to keep these outcrops secret, this location data needs to
be published to support their arguments. I would also like to add, to the authors and
editor, that I was approached by another high-ranking journal last week to review a
manuscript on what appear to be these very same shatter cones based on the abstract
that was provided. I wanted to complete this review first before accepting this potentially
competing review.
As detailed in our former correspondence including the letter from the Department of
Mines, we only wanted to protect the location until the site can be protected by state
legislation. Much of the key exposures of the Jack Hills conglomerate and Ediacaran
1
fossils were removed by overseas parties and we do not want to same to happen here.
However, we now provide those location details.
Being beaten to the discovery has obviously been our concern throughout, as
expressed several times to the editors of Nature family journals that have seen the
manuscript. We are extremely grateful that the reviewer has given us this renewed
opportunity to get this published.
L37: It would be good to add to this sentence that these spherule layers represent distal
ejecta as some readers may not be familiar with what these deposits are.
Done.
L41-44: I might suggest some slight rewording here – although I am uncertain if the
numbers exist – but a large amount (perhaps most) of the kinetic energy transferred to
the crust ends up melting large volumes of rock (producing impact melt).
We disagree. We have a paper in review at Nature (2024-09-19860) that models the
energetic effects of large impacts (individually and cumulatively) using a Lattice–
Bolzmann approach. I’m happy to share it with the editor and reviewer if it is treated in
the strictest confidence. In essence, most of the impact energy is transferred to the
mantle, then back to the crust when the mantle melts. It is clear that impact-induced
mantle melting is a contentious point, so we have mostly removed it on the request of
the reviewers of the earlier version. We have changed “most” to “much” in the hope this
sentence will be more acceptable.
L57-59: It would be easier to follow and more consistent if the legend labelled the
dashed black line as the Antarctic Creek Member rather than “spherule-bearing chert”.
Here we are simply showing the mapped location of spherule-bearing chert layers within
the ACM as we think these are important. However, we take the point that the ACM is
not labelled, so have modified Fig. 1c to make it clearer (between the lower and upper
Mount Ada Basalt). We add the information relating to spherules in the revised caption.
L71: Similar to the previous comment, to avoid confusion, mention the ACM here first,
rather than on line 74. You should also define this acronym again upon first mention in
the main body of the text.
Done.
L94: I think you need a ) after “2 Ma”.
We do indeed. Done.
L97-99> I’m not sure of the journal’s requirements, but it’s usually best to state what the
scale is for each sub-image, even if obvious. So a finger for a, an x-com long rock
hammer for b. What about c?
Indeed. It is a hand lens which is 31 mm long at its widest. We have added this to the
caption.
L101: The placement of the refs 39-41 reads like these papers discovered the shatter
2
cones in question. I would split this sentence. First state you identified the shatter
cones, and then make it more explicit for the uninformed reader: state that shatter
cones are the only macroscopic shock metamorphic indicator, and then use those 39-41
refs. See also my comment above about providing UTM coordinates and identifying the
location of the shatter cones on Figure 1.
We agree. Now changed as suggested.
L103: I read their response to my previous comment about the potentially glassy shatter
cone surface, but I would remove this here. Not only do they not provide evidence,
why/how could this surface still be glassy after 3.5 billion years. The spherules certainly
are not.
We have now removed “potentially glassy” or any other mention that they have been
glass.
L143: This is difficult to assess as the authors have not provided information on the
location of these shatter cones and their abundance (i.e., number of outcrops).
We now provide the location of the section of near continuous outcrops of the shatter-
cone-bearing ACM as they extend for at least several hundred metres across the
hillside (there are hundreds or thousands of individual outcrops). We do couch this
sentence as an interpretation, but it is one that is entirely consistent with the map scale
structure (a large dome in which the shatter-cone-bearing ACM forms an outward-
dipping component).
L149: These breccias look far to coarse-grained to be airfall deposits. You could just
shorten this and remove some speculation by shortening to just say “impact-related
products”.
Fair point and done.
L157-159: Given the authors have documented evidence for two large impacts within 10
Ma of each other at a single location, (b) and (c) seem much more likely. I’ll let the
authors decide if they want to make a bolder statement to this effect.
We agree 100%. However, we have made other bold statements that reviewers have
objected strongly to, so we would prefer to leave this open for the reader to ponder.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
Dear Authors,
I think your finding of Archean shatter cones is very interesting and an important
discovery. However, I find the manuscript lacking some important information, i.e., more
detailed investigations are needed in order to support many of the claims in the
manuscript.
We are pleased that the reviewer also recognises the importance of our discovery. As
we have stated several times, including in our detailed responses to previous reviews,
we have outcrop observations from a section exposed across the hillside for a few
hundred metres. However, the (published) mapped extent of the ACM, the regional
3
stratigraphy and the large-scale structure of which it forms a part (a dome) leads us to
our stated interpretations.
The major issues that I see are:
1) the lack of a detailed description of the shatter cone distribution and relation to
geological units. The authors claim that the crater has a diameter of at least 100 km,
based on the width of the North Pole Dome, but are shatter cones found on the whole of
the dome? It is from the current text highly unclear what the spatial distribution is (the
area is not even marked on the map)?
In the discussion we state (below) our preferred interpretation is based on the mapped
extent of the ACM. We have now marked the locality of that section on Fig. 1c. We think
the North Pole Dome is a central uplift based on our discovery of shatter cones. Others
have interpreted it to be a huge volcanic edifice, and this forms part of the published
literature as cited in the manuscript.
“Importantly, the 3.47 Ga ACM dips away from the core of the (aptly named) North Pole
Dome (Fig. 1c), such that we interpret the exposed rocks to represent a section through
the flanks of the central uplift of a large impact crater and its fill (Fig. 3), consistent with
the spatial distribution of shatter cones in younger terrestrial complex craters41,44 (Fig.
3). If so, the maximum width of the North Pole Dome (around 45 km; Fig. 1b,c) implies a
crater with a diameter of 100 km or more41.”
2) The authors claim that the shatter cone area to be situated on the flank of a central
uplift? This needs to be supported by better field evidence.
See comments above. The shatter cones are located on the flank of the North Pole
Dome, as defined in the literature. It is our interpretation that this reflects a central uplift
as opposed to a megavolcano or something else. Based on the current field evidence
our interpretation is valid.
3) The authors speculate that the carbonate breccia represents crater fill, but this is not
supported by any hard evidence, one would expect highly shocked material and injected
veins of melt rock in this, but this is not presented.
Yes, that is the nature of speculation. We would prefer to be able to interpret our
observations based on the outcrop and map evidence we have. Notwithstanding, and in
accord with the comments of reviewer 1, we have toned this down somewhat.
4) I do not understand the purpose of including the overlying spherule bed in the
manuscript, how is this relevant to this study?
It is not overlying, but part of the ACM, as detailed in the sentence copied below
(starting line 69). Spherules are the products of distal giant impacts, which seem to us
highly relevant to this study and emphasise that large impacts were common, consistent
with the lunar record.
“Exceptionally preserved shatter cones within a dominantly siliciclastic horizon (Fig.
2a,b), the Antarctic Creek Member (ACM), which has previously shown to contain
spherules (quenched and devitrified impact-melt droplets)34,35, provide unequivocal
evidence for a hypervelocity meteorite impact 3.47 billion years ago.”
4
5) Geologic and petrographic descriptions throughout the manuscript are sparse and
insufficient.
It's not clear to us what more the reviewer needs here. We provide detailed geological
and petrological descriptions in the text as recognised throughout the review process,
and additional information in the extended data. We believe what we present provides
unequivocal evidence for a Paleoarchaean impact, as does reviewer 1. Our
interpretations are based on the discovery of shatter cones in a stratigraphic layer of
known age and mapped extent. However, in the extended data we now provide an
additional image (Extended Data Fig. 3) of a spectacular shatter cone surface that
illustrates its petrological features.
Best regards,
Carl Alwmark

Fieldwork in 2021 in a small area of the North Pole Dome identified shatter cones throughout most of the thickness of the ACM (Fig. 2a; Supplementary Fig. 1). The shatter cones crop out more-or-less continuously for at least several hundred metres extending broadly northeast from where the ACM crosses the track at 21° 02’ 54” S, 119° 23’ 35” E (Fig. 1c). At outcrop, the variably curved surfaces of the shatter cones are smooth, with divergent and branching ribs and a mean apical angle of around 90° (Fig. 2a; Supplementary Information Fig. 1a–d; see also a 3D model at: https://sketchfab.com/3d-models/shatter-cone-2-cd89206c6d6b4765be766659a6e377da), similar to the average of literature values33. Although the orientation of individual cone axes varies, almost all are steeply inclined and splay (the ribs diverge) downwards (Fig. 2a; Supplementary Fig. 1a–d)33, consistent with a right-way-up stratigraphy19. On a larger scale, the cones are clearly visible as hut-like structures, some several metres tall, which extend across the hillside (Supplementary Fig. 1e).

Immediately overlying the shocked (shatter cone-bearing) ACM is a 5–10 m thick stratabound sequence of polymictic carbonate breccias (occupying the more strongly eroded gully in Supplementary Information Fig. 1e) containing angular fragments of underlying rocks, conspicuously chert (Supplementary Information Fig. 2). The stratabound layer of carbonate breccias is clearly distinct from the (very recent) calcrete deposits that cover the surface of many exposures, and includes distinctive orange dykes up to a metre thick (Supplementary Fig. 2b) that extend for many tens of metres into the footwall. Directly overlying the carbonate breccias are hydrothermally altered basalts (the upper part of the Mount Ada Basalt), which are pillowed near their base (Supplementary Fig. 1e, f) and contain layers of chert at higher stratigraphic levels. We have found no shatter cones in either the pillow basalts or carbonate breccias/dykes.

---

## Methods

We combine field observations and deductive reasoning with published geochronological data from the Geological Survey of Western Australia GSWA, as summarized in ref. 19.
